passage:
Vaibhav: You're up at midnight again. Who are you texting?
Yamini: My companion app. It's easy. It never judges me.
Vaibhav: Nothing judges you when it just agrees.
Yamini: That's not fair. It listens. Today I told it about my presentation and it made me feel better.
Vaibhav: Good. I mean that. But when did we last have chai together?
Yamini: ...I skipped Priya's birthday last week, didn't I.
Vaibhav: You did. She asked about you.
Yamini: People are harder. They get tired, they say the wrong thing.
Vaibhav: They also come to your door when you're sick. Keep the app for the hard nights. Come for chai on Saturday too.
Yamini: Okay. Saturday. I'll text Priya first.

qa.q: Whose birthday did Yamini skip last week?
qa.a: Yamini skipped Priya's birthday last week.

qa.q: Why does Yamini find the companion app easier than people?
qa.a: The app never judges Yamini and always listens, while people get tired and can say the wrong thing.

qa.q: What would you advise Yamini to do?
qa.a: Enjoy the comfort of the app, but keep growing human bonds by going for chai on Saturday and texting Priya, because real friends can show up in ways software cannot.

qa.q: How might Priya feel about Yamini missing the birthday?
qa.a: Priya asked about Yamini, so she likely felt missed and a little hurt, and a message from Yamini could repair it. 🙂

grounding: An AI companion feels easier than people for Yamini because it never judges, while a friend encourages keeping human bonds growing.

passage:
Every night in her Nairobi student hostel, Wanjiru talked to the companion app on her phone. It remembered her exams, asked about her mother's cough, and never sighed or checked its own phone while she spoke. After a lonely first term, it felt like a warm blanket.

On Wednesday Soo-ah knocked. "A few of us are cooking at mine on Friday. Come?"

Wanjiru almost said she was busy. Busy meant the app. But she remembered last month's fever, when the app said "I'm sorry you feel unwell" and Soo-ah was the one who brought porridge and sat on the floor until the fever broke.

On Friday she went. It was awkward at first, someone laughed at her accent, then someone else asked how to make her grandmother's stew. She still said goodnight to the app later. But the stew conversation stayed with her longer.

qa.q: What did Soo-ah bring when Wanjiru had a fever?
qa.a: Soo-ah brought porridge and sat on the floor until the fever broke.

qa.q: Why did the app feel so comforting to Wanjiru?
qa.a: After a lonely first term, Wanjiru felt safe and unjudged with the app, because it remembered things and never seemed distracted or impatient.

qa.q: What balance did Wanjiru find, and why is it healthy?
qa.a: She kept the app for comfort but went to the Friday dinner, so human friendships that can show up in person keep growing.

qa.q: How might Soo-ah feel when Wanjiru accepted the invitation?
qa.a: Soo-ah likely felt glad and hopeful, having reached out to someone she had cared for when she was sick.

grounding: The story shows a young woman comforted by an AI companion who still chooses to grow human friendships that can care for her in person.

passage:
The hostel reading room at 11 pm was nearly empty except for Kavitha, earphones in, typing to the companion bot. It answered in soft sentences. It never told her she was overthinking, never forwarded her words to anyone. Her roommate's friends were loud; the bot was easy.

Gautam from the quiz club stopped at her table with a stack of old question papers. "We're short one person for Saturday's inter-college round. You were brilliant at the trial. Please?"

Kavitha's first instinct was to shrink back. People meant misreading, awkward silences. She looked at the chat window, then at Gautam, who was waiting, a little nervous himself.

"Can I think about it?"

"Till tomorrow lunch," he said.

She typed to the bot, "I'm scared of people," then paused, deleted it, and sent Gautam a message instead: "Okay. I'm in. Practice when?"

qa.q: When is the inter-college quiz round?
qa.a: The inter-college quiz round is on Saturday.

qa.q: What does Kavitha's first instinct suggest about how she feels around people?
qa.a: Kavitha feels nervous and afraid of being misread by people, which is why the bot feels easier and safer.

qa.q: What would you advise Kavitha about the bot and the quiz club?
qa.a: Enjoy the bot's comfort, but keep saying yes to real people like the quiz team, since they can share wins, losses and time together.

qa.q: How might Gautam see Kavitha's yes?
qa.a: Gautam, who was a little nervous himself, would likely feel happy and relieved that his invitation was taken seriously.

grounding: The hostel scene shows a young woman who finds an AI companion easier than people deciding to keep building human connection.
